facts.statement: The genus Protodontopteryx contains only one known species, Protodontopteryx ruthae.
facts.quote: It contains one species, Protodontopteryx ruthae.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was collected in New Zealand's Canterbury Region on November 11, 2017, by fossil hunter Leigh Love.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of Protodontopteryx ruthae, CM 2018.124.8, was collected in the Canterbury Region of New Zealand on 11 November 2017 by Leigh Love.

facts.statement: The species was formally described in 2019 by a team including Gerald Mayr, Vanesa L. De Pietri, Leigh Love, Al Mannering, and Richard Paul Scofield.
facts.quote: In 2019, Protodontopteryx ruthae was described by Gerald Mayr, Vanesa L. De Pietri, Leigh Love, Al Mannering, and Richard Paul Scofield.

facts.statement: The species name honors Ruth Love, the wife of the collector Leigh Love.
facts.quote: The specific name honors Ruth Love, the wife of the fossil's collector Leigh Love.

facts.statement: Protodontopteryx had an estimated wingspan of about 1 meter, making it roughly the size of an average gull.
facts.quote: With an estimated wingspan of about 1 m, Protodontopteryx was the size of an average gull—much smaller than all post-Paleocene pelagornithids.

facts.statement: The beak was deeper at the base and tapered more strongly toward the tip compared to other pelagornithids.
facts.quote: The beak was similar in relative length to that of other pelagornithids, but was deeper at the base and therefore tapered more strongly toward the tip.

facts.statement: Its external nostrils were larger and more similar to those of albatrosses than the reduced nostrils found in later pelagornithids.
facts.quote: The external nostrils were larger than the very reduced nostrils of other pelagornithids, and were more similar in size and position to those of albatrosses.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Protodontopteryx was less pelagic than later relatives, as its larger nostrils were likely less adapted for saltwater immersion.
facts.quote: This suggests Protodontopteryx was less pelagic than later pelagornithids (many living aequornithean seabirds have reduced external nostrils to protect the nasal cavity against saltwater).

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Protodontopteryx may have been mainly piscivorous, whereas later species likely foraged for squid and molluscs.
facts.quote: The short pseudoteeth of Protodontopteryx, contrasted with the more fragile needle-like pseudoteeth of later pelagornithids, may indicate a dietary shift in the family's evolution: Protodontopteryx may have been mainly piscivorous, while later species foraged for squid and other molluscs.

facts.statement: During the early Paleocene, New Zealand had a tropical climate with sea temperatures of about 25 degrees Celsius.
facts.quote: During the early Paleocene when Protodontopteryx lived, New Zealand had a tropical climate with a sea temperature of about 25 C.

facts.statement: Protodontopteryx belongs to the family Pelagornithidae.
The time range for Protodontopteryx is estimated between 61.66 and 59.24 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Selandian to Selandian (61.66 to 59.24 million years ago)
